clinicalPearls: Presents with bilateral, symmetric, painless and slowly progressive visual loss with a central or centrocaecal scotoma and prominent dyschromatopsia.
Key deficiencies include vitamin B12, folate, thiamine, pyridoxine, riboflavin and copper, often on a background of protein-calorie malnutrition.
Important settings are chronic alcohol misuse, bariatric surgery, malabsorption, highly restrictive diets and famine, and combined nutritional and toxic injury is common.
Red-green colour vision is disturbed early and disproportionately to the level of acuity.
The disc is normal or mildly hyperaemic early and develops temporal pallor as the papillomacular bundle atrophies.
Pupillary light responses are relatively preserved and a relative afferent pupillary defect is absent when involvement is symmetric.
Early recognition and repletion, including empirical thiamine in at-risk patients, can reverse or arrest visual loss.
A hereditary mitochondrial optic neuropathy such as Leber hereditary optic neuropathy can mimic the picture and should be considered.
reference.pathophysiology: The small-calibre fibres of the papillomacular bundle have exceptionally high metabolic demand and depend on efficient mitochondrial oxidative phosphorylation. B-group vitamins act as cofactors in the enzymatic pathways generating cellular energy, so their deficiency impairs adenosine triphosphate production, disrupts axonal transport and myelin maintenance, and increases oxidative stress. These fibres are therefore selectively vulnerable, producing the characteristic central and centrocaecal field loss, with copper deficiency causing an analogous metabolic injury.
additionalDifferentials: Compressive optic neuropathy or chiasmal lesion
Maculopathy such as occult macular dystrophy
additionalInvestigations: Serum vitamin B12 with folate and red-cell folate
Thiamine and serum copper with caeruloplasmin
Full blood count and blood film looking for macrocytosis
Magnetic resonance imaging to exclude a compressive or chiasmal lesion
Automated perimetry and colour vision testing
Optical coherence tomography of the retinal nerve fibre layer
Mitochondrial DNA testing for Leber hereditary optic neuropathy where suspected
redFlags: Rapidly progressive or markedly asymmetric loss, prompting reconsideration of a compressive or other cause
Accompanying neurological signs or features of Wernicke encephalopathy
Failure to improve after adequate nutritional repletion
Coexisting toxic exposure that may accelerate the injury
reference.prognosis: The outcome is variable and depends on the duration of deficiency; vision may recover substantially with early repletion. Prolonged, untreated deficiency leads to optic atrophy and permanent visual impairment.
pitfalls: Attributing loss to alcohol alone without measuring B12 and folate
Overlooking a coexisting toxic contribution to the neuropathy
Delaying thiamine replacement in at-risk or alcohol-dependent patients
Failing to consider copper deficiency, for example after bariatric surgery or with excess zinc intake
references: American Academy of Ophthalmology, Basic and Clinical Science Course, Neuro-Ophthalmology
